q: You run `StandardScaler(inputCol="num_vec", outputCol="num_scaled")` with no other options. What does each value become?
e: Spark's StandardScaler defaults to `withMean=False, withStd=True`: it only divides by the standard deviation. Set `withMean=True` for real z-scores.

q: Why does Spark's StandardScaler not center the data by default?
o: Centering changes the order of the values
The mean cannot be computed in a distributed way
Subtracting the mean turns sparse vectors into dense ones, which can use a lot of memory
Centering is only needed for tree models
e: A sparse vector stores only non-zero values. After subtracting the mean almost every entry is non-zero, so the vector becomes dense.

q: A scaler is fit on the training set and applied to the test set. The test set's scaled mean is 0.04 and its standard deviation 1.01. What does this mean?
o: This is expected: the test set is scaled with the training statistics
The scaler was fit on the wrong data
The test set must be refit to get exactly 0 and 1
The scaler failed and must be rerun with `withStd=False`
e: Only the data the scaler was fit on lands exactly at 0 and 1. Test rows reuse the training μ and σ, so their statistics are close but not exact. That keeps the evaluation honest.

q: A column has a few extreme values caused by a unit error you cannot fix yet. Which scaler keeps the normal values spread out best?
e: RobustScaler uses the median and the interquartile range, which barely move when a few extreme values are added. Min and max, and the standard deviation, are pulled by the outliers.

q: For which model is scaling the numeric features usually unnecessary?
e: Tree splits compare a feature with a threshold, and rescaling moves the threshold with the values, so the same split is found. Distance-based, gradient-based and regularized models are scale-sensitive.
